original_value: Information regarding the shape and depth of a landslide sliding surface (LSS) is fundamental for the estimation of the volume of the unstable masses, which in turn is of primary importance for the assessment of landslide magnitude and risk scenarios as well as in refining stability analyses. To assess an LSS is not an easy task and is generally time-consuming and expensive. In this work, a method existing in the literature, based on the inclination of movement vectors along a cross-section to estimate the depth and geometry LSSs, is used for the first time while exploiting satellite interferometric data. Given the advent of satellite interferometric data and the related increasing availability of spatially dense and accurate measurements, we test the effectiveness of this method—here named the vector inclination method (VIM)—to four case landslides located in Italy characterized by different types of movement, kinematics and volume. Geotechnical and geophysical information of the LSS is used to validate the method. Our results show that each of the presented cases provides useful insight into the validity of VIM using satellite interferometric data. The main advantages of VIM applied to satellite interferometry are that it enables estimation of the LSS with a theoretical worldwide coverage, as well as with no need for onsite instrumentation or even direct access; however, a good density of measurement points in both ascending and descending geometry is necessary. The combined use of VIM and traditional investigations can provide a more accurate LSS model.

result.paraphrase: Understanding the shape and depth of a landslide sliding surface (LSS) is essential for estimating the volume of unstable masses, which is crucial for evaluating landslide magnitude and risk scenarios and for improving stability analyses. Assessing an LSS is difficult and typically time-consuming and costly. In this study, a literature-based method that uses the inclination of movement vectors along a cross-section to estimate LSS depth and geometry is applied for the first time using satellite interferometric data. Taking advantage of the growing availability of spatially dense, accurate satellite interferometric measurements, we test the method—here called the vector inclination method (VIM)—on four landslides in Italy with different movement types, kinematics, and volumes. The LSS is validated using geotechnical and geophysical information. Our results indicate that each case offers valuable insight into the validity of VIM when used with satellite interferometric data. The main advantages of applying VIM to satellite interferometry are its potential for worldwide coverage and the lack of need for onsite instrumentation or direct access; however, it requires a good density of measurement points in both ascending and descending geometry. Combining VIM with traditional investigations can yield a more accurate LSS model.
